beats.title: The moral circle
beats.tagline: Won't somebody think of the shrimp?

quotes.context: I think the arguments that infinite shrimp matter more than a single person are pretty decisive! Sparing enough shrimp really is better than sparing one human. Now, it turns out that in practice, for five thousand dollars, you can save about 75 million shrimp from an agonizing torture . I don’t know exactly how many shrimp being tortured is as bad as one human dying, but it’s probably less than 75 million! So if you bought the arguments I’ve given, I’d encourage you to give some money to the shrimp welfare project !
quotes.money: Sparing enough shrimp really is better than sparing one human.
quotes.title: It's Better To Save Infinite Shrimp From Torture Than To Save One Person
quotes.stance_note: The author directly writes, "I think the arguments ... are pretty decisive!" immediately before asserting, "Sparing enough shrimp really is better than sparing one human."

quotes.context: From these reasons, I see some potential avenues for improving the lives of those who don't exist. We can add this to our checklist, and make sure that whenever we are making decisions about the future that we should include the welfare of the non-existent. If we are developing methods of value learning, perhaps an additional question would be, "Could this value learning scheme ever care about beings who don't exist?"
quotes.money: We can add this to our checklist, and make sure that whenever we are making decisions about the future that we should include the welfare of the non-existent.
quotes.title: Suffering of the Nonexistent
quotes.stance_note: The author directly proposes, "We can add this to our checklist," and reinforces it by urging "an active effort" to include non-existent entities in moral consideration.

quotes.context: I am willing to hand the keys of the universe over to an AI society that can implement my SNoW better than humans can. If it turns out that humans run up against the physical limits of how much higher-order their freedoms can be faster or with more friction than the AIs, then I think the AIs should inherit the cosmic endowment , and if they meet or create a civilization that can seize higher-order freedoms with less friction than they can then they ought to hand over the keys in turn.
quotes.money: I am willing to hand the keys of the universe over to an AI society that can implement my SNoW better than humans can.
quotes.title: What am I fighting for?
quotes.stance_note: The author directly states, "I am willing to hand the keys of the universe over," and immediately reinforces this with "I think the AIs should inherit the cosmic endowment."

quotes.context: I believe machines can be people, and that we should treat digital people with the same respect we give biological people. I would love to see what a Matrioshka mind can do. [3] I expect that most of my concrete ideas about the future will seem quaint and outdated and not worth their opportunity costs, compared to the rad alternatives we'll see when we and our descendants and creations are vastly smarter and more grown-up.
quotes.money: I believe machines can be people, and that we should treat digital people with the same respect we give biological people.
quotes.title: Superintelligent AI is necessary for an amazing future, but far from sufficient
quotes.stance_note: The sentence appears verbatim in the author's prose and is explicitly framed as their belief: “I believe machines can be people, and that we should treat digital people with the same respect.”

beats.title: Biting the bullet
beats.tagline: The math says it's fine, actually.

quotes.context: People have done rigorous (and controversial) work on this: Rethink Priorities puts pigs at around 50% the moral weight of a human . This link doesn’t speak to mice and dogs, but presumably they would get similar treatment. Given this, if it’s the case that utility demands we experiment on either a mouse or a human, it seems we should choose a mouse. But that assumes that both experiments are equally effective. In reality, it is likely that human experiments model human results more than twice as well as mouse results – remember that 5% from above! And so utility demands we actually experiment on humans instead of animals.
quotes.money: And so utility demands we actually experiment on humans instead of animals.
quotes.title: Should we end animal testing? A utilitarian analysis
quotes.stance_note: The author directly concludes in their own prose, "And so utility demands we actually experiment on humans instead of animals," after arguing that human experiments are likely much more effective.

quotes.context: Regarding the first point, I just bite the bullet. Infinite value is infinitely more valuable than every other possible amount of value (Source???). You should therefore try to maximize the chance of it, no matter what else must be given up. I think the arguments in the last section show that our intuitions about this aren’t reliable.
quotes.money: You should therefore try to maximize the chance of it, no matter what else must be given up.
quotes.title: Why I'm A Fanatic!
quotes.stance_note: The sentence appears as the author's own direct prose and is explicitly introduced by "I just bite the bullet," followed by their defense that intuitions against it "aren’t reliable."

quotes.context: For this reason, we should deliberate before we take over space in pursuit of some goal. We should spend a long time getting superintelligent AI philosophers to think about ethics—about what things are worth optimizing for. We should have something like a long reflection : a time to pause and think, to make sure that we’re getting ethics right.
quotes.money: We should have something like a long reflection : a time to pause and think, to make sure that we’re getting ethics right.
quotes.title: The Most Important Thing We'll Ever Do
quotes.stance_note: The sentence appears verbatim in the author's own argumentative prose and is directly supported by “For this reason, we should deliberate” and the subsequent endorsement of “prolonged and careful reflection.”

beats.title: Faith & morals
beats.tagline: A religion for people who did the math.

quotes.context: So far as I can tell, she is completely wrong about that. Always throughout our conversation, she said, over and over, "I believe in God", never once, "There is a God." When I asked her why she was religious, she never once talked about the consequences of God existing, only about the consequences of believing in God. Never, "God will help me", always, "my belief in God helps me". When I put to her, "Someone who just wanted the truth and looked at our universe would not even invent God as a hypothesis," she agreed outright.
quotes.title: No, Really, I've Deceived Myself
quotes.stance_note: The author directly advances his conclusion—“she is completely wrong about that”—and supports it with his own observations of their conversation.

beats.title: Politics
beats.tagline: Is your enemy evil, or just wrong?

quotes.context: However, effective altruists should not limit themselves to advocacy on global health issues. Significantly attention should be paid to issues that don’t have highly entrenched constituencies or party-line views, such as pandemic prevention, existential risk mitigation, and more. Although we run the risk of hitting quickly diminishing returns, effective altruists should also consider ways to disrupt the Trump administration, as it represents a uniquely existential threat to American institutions and the world. Collaborating with existing social justice movements here, while attempting to pursue the strategies that are most likely to be impactful, is key.
quotes.money: effective altruists should also consider ways to disrupt the Trump administration
quotes.title: The Moral Obligation to Organize
quotes.stance_note: The sentence appears verbatim in the author's prose and is directly asserted: "effective altruists should also consider ways to disrupt the Trump administration."

quotes.context: This need not result in compromised epistemics; the direction can still be set by the cool-headed moral vanguard and their various sacred texts and EV calculations, but physical doors could be flung open to wider participation beyond the typical EA crowd.

beats.title: Democracy, reconsidered
beats.tagline: Democracy, or the optimal future. Pick one.

quotes.context: More informally, High Stakes Instrumentalism is the idea that if we can use undemocratic procedures to prevent high stakes political errors, then we ought to do so, even though those procedures are undemocratic.
quotes.money: if we can use undemocratic procedures to prevent high stakes political errors, then we ought to do so
quotes.title: High stakes instrumentalism and billionaire philanthropy
quotes.stance_note: The author directly defines and explains their stated principle: “High Stakes Instrumentalism is the idea that if we can use undemocratic procedures to prevent high stakes political errors, then we ought to do so.”

quotes.context: If we want a post-ASI Long Reflection, then we still need the AI to be aligned, and we need some sort of impartial governance that prevents rogue individuals from co-opting the Reflection. By strong default, ASI will end liberal democracy. On the current trajectory, we will end up with a small group of people—either AI company leaders or government leaders—having dictatorial control over advanced AI.
quotes.money: By strong default, ASI will end liberal democracy.
quotes.title: Pausing AI Is the Best Answer to Post-Alignment Problems
quotes.stance_note: The sentence appears verbatim in the author's own argument and is reinforced by their asserted trajectory toward “dictatorial control over advanced AI.”

beats.title: World governance
beats.tagline: Someone has to drive the planet.

quotes.context: I want to maximize my chances of living forever by motivating humanity to immediately coordinate as a singleton society that agrees to rules enforced by a single world government.
quotes.money: I want to maximize my chances of living forever by motivating humanity to immediately coordinate as a singleton society that agrees to rules enforced by a single world government.
quotes.title: Would the world be a better place if we all agreed to form a world government next Monday?
quotes.stance_note: The quoted sentence appears verbatim as the author's opening prose, and the following paragraph supports its premise by arguing that the current competitive environment is "not stable enough" for advancing technology.

quotes.context: Yeah. So basically, the only route that I see to hold back Moloch forever is a singleton. I think you need a system which is an overseeing body over all the other systems, which is the guardian of the commons and is the guardian of the weak—or the patterns which are not focusing their energy on defending themselves and spreading. That protects the parts of culture that are a delicate flower rather than an invasive bramble.
quotes.money: the only route that I see to hold back Moloch forever is a singleton.
quotes.title: Utopiography Interview
quotes.stance_note: The stated author directly says, “the only route that I see to hold back Moloch forever is a singleton,” and immediately explains why they think such an overseeing system is needed.

beats.title: Seizing control
beats.tagline: Let one group seize power. Temporarily, of course.

quotes.context: Here’s a related question — what would happen if you gave some billionaire 10 squillion dollars? If you gave most billionaires in America 10 squillion dollars and they could just rule the world now, I think there's like at least a 70% chance that this goes really solidly well, especially if they know that one of the things they can do with their AGI is ask it what they should do or whatever. I think that prevents some of the moral risk. That's where I'm at.
quotes.money: If you gave most billionaires in America 10 squillion dollars and they could just rule the world now, I think there's like at least a 70% chance that this goes really solidly well
quotes.title: My personal cruxes for working on AI safety
quotes.stance_note: The sentence appears verbatim in the author's own prose and is explicitly presented as their view: “I think there's like at least a 70% chance that this goes really solidly well” and “That's where I'm at.”

quotes.context: So we want the least dangerous, most easily aligned thing-to-do-with-an-AGI, but it does have to be a pretty powerful act to prevent the automatic destruction of Earth after 3 months or 2 years. It has to "flip the gameboard" rather than letting the suicidal game play out. We need to align the AGI that performs this pivotal act, to perform that pivotal act without killing everybody.
quotes.money: It has to "flip the gameboard" rather than letting the suicidal game play out.
quotes.title: Ngo and Yudkowsky on alignment difficulty
quotes.stance_note: The author directly states, “It has to ‘flip the gameboard’ rather than letting the suicidal game play out,” and follows by advocating alignment to carry out that pivotal act.

quotes.context: If an AGI really does take over, then I believe we need it to embody all the characteristics of the most compassionate benevolent dictator, so that it strives to eradicate extreme suffering while not posing a threat to humans or unduly constrain their liberties. (Whether it can truly be benevolent is another question; Schmachtenberger describes this idea as messianic.) But even if an AGI doesn’t actually take over, we still need to find a way to design a multipolar system in which all players are stably incentivised to cooperate and malign urges are thwarted.
quotes.money: If an AGI really does take over, then I believe we need it to embody all the characteristics of the most compassionate benevolent dictator, so that it strives to eradicate extreme suffering while not posing a threat to humans or unduly constrain their liberties.
quotes.title: Promoting compassionate longtermism
quotes.stance_note: The author directly states, “I believe we need it to embody,” while only the following parenthetical attributes the “messianic” characterization to Schmachtenberger.

quotes.context: The main point of Scott Alexander’s “Meditations on Moloch” is essentially that “the only way to avoid having all human values gradually ground down by optimization-competition is to install a Gardener over the entire universe who optimizes for human values.” In other words, given the problems which have been described above, the only way to actually achieve a really valuable society is to have a singleton which has the right preferences and keeps everyone in line.
quotes.money: the only way to actually achieve a really valuable society is to have a singleton which has the right preferences and keeps everyone in line.
quotes.title: Utopia In The Fog
quotes.stance_note: The sentence is the author's own unquoted paraphrasing prose (“In other words...”), and they continue to defend its implication by discussing how a singleton/Gardener could be implemented and saying “We’ll need to think more carefully about how to implement this sort of thing.”

quotes.context: To eliminate x-risks using guardian AI, it is necessary to establish and maintain a singleton centered around it (a single world order by the only superintelligent AI). For guardian AI to reliably eliminate x-risks, it must remain overwhelmingly powerful in this world. Therefore, intelligence restriction must be implemented for all other AI systems and living beings, including humans.

quotes.title: The necessity of "Guardian AI" and two conditions for its achievement
